transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-12-12 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~58m | Attendees: Jamie, Marisol, Diego (Redwood) / Alex, Priya, Sam, Lina (HeliosRotor)

Summary: quick partner intro, discuss channel model (reseller vs managed onramp), hardware compatibility for on‑prem blades, initial pilot ideas and security/compliance + next steps.

00:00 Jamie: All right, hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jamie Park, I'm the AE on the Redwood side, with Marisol and Diego. How's things over there?
00:12 Alex: Hey Jamie, yep, thanks. Alex here, CTO at HeliosRotor. A little jetlag but all good.
00:18 Priya: Priya here — excited to talk partner models and, uh, how we might integrate your runtime into our channel.
00:25 Jamie: Great. Quick agenda: introductions, high level partner models, compatibility questions for your GPU blades, security/compliance checklist, and then propose next steps / pilot. Sound ok?
00:34 Priya: Yep sounds good.
00:36 Marisol: Quick note — I can drive the technical compatibility part. I'll try to sketch what needs to look like for Redwood Dedicated vs Redwood Private.
00:45 Sam: Sam speaking, I'm infra lead — we'll focus on driver stacks, interconnect and how the runtime sits with our provisioning tooling.
00:52 Diego: Also I'll follow up on test harness details and perf expectations.
01:00 Jamie: Cool. Priya, can you tell us why HeliosRotor is interested in Redwood— from a business angle — and what customers you're targeting in the channel?
01:10 Priya: Sure. We're a hardware vendor building multi‑node GPU blades — our go‑to‑market has been OEM and system integrators. We're seeing demand from cloud providers and enterprises that want a managed onramp for inference. So thinking: offer customers a pre‑validated stack (hardware + Redwood runtime) either as a co‑managed bundle or as a reseller offering.
01:30 Alex: The core ask: low‑latency at scale for text gen workloads, predictable cost for inference, and a path for some customers to run fully on‑prem.
01:40 Jamie: That maps well to our product lines. Hosted API is fastest to market, Redwood Dedicated is reserved capacity on Redwood infra, and Redwood Private is what we deploy into customer VPCs or on prem. For channel, two typical patterns we see: 1) reseller / marketplace listing (we publish images and a validated config) or 2) onramp partnership where your customers get a managed install of Redwood Private on HeliosRotor hardware.
02:05 Sam: For onprem installs — we're concerned about kernel/driver compatibility, container runtimes, and our fleet orchestrator (we run a modified k8s distro). How invasive is Redwood Private?
02:15 Marisol: Short answer: Redwood Private is a control plane + runtime that can be deployed into your environment. It requires a small agent and GPU drivers. On the runtime side we have a GPU‑optimized inference engine — it uses kernel-level optimizations when possible but we generally ship compatible docker images. There are a few gotchas — e.g., CUDA/ROCm versions, NCCL for multi‑node, and our quant path expects certain kernel support.
02:40 Sam: Got it. Do you support mixed nvlink / PCIe topologies? Our blades have NVLink across pairs and PCIe fabric between blades.
02:49 Diego: Yes, we can work with mixed topologies. Our runtime will prefer NVLink for KV cache and sharded attention where available; otherwise fall back to PCIe. We do need a topology map and RDMA/NCCL config.
03:05 Alex: When you say KV cache — I think previous notes said "k V cash" in a doc we received — what's the expectation there? Does Redwood persist cache across restarts?
03:15 Marisol: Sorry transcription baby — KV cache (key‑value cache) for decoder states. We have options: ephemeral in‑memory cache which is fastest, or a persisted cache that can be checkpointed for long‑running sessions. For a channel offering, ephemeral is default; for certain enterprise use cases we support persistent checkpointing to NFS or object store.
03:36 Lina: On security: we need to understand key management, encryption at rest, audit logs and SSO.
03:42 Jamie: Absolutely. We integrate with KMS providers and HSMs for key management in Redwood Private. We support SAML/SSO, RBAC, and provide audit logs + metrics. We'll share our SOC2 docs and architecture whitepaper.
03:58 Priya: Do you have any specific partner onboarding programs, like co‑marketing, training or enablement?
04:04 Jamie: Yes — partnerships PM will work with you on joint GTM motions, training, and a technical validation kit. We'll also provide a partner playbook that outlines validated hardware lists, recommended driver stacks, and billing models.
04:18 Priya: Nice. Let's talk about the commercial model quickly — are you expecting channel margins or commit tiers?
04:24 Jamie: We typically do committed reserved capacity for Dedicated, and partner discounts / margin splits for reseller flows. For onprem installations, there's a Private license + support fee; we can do volume commit discounts. We'll send sample pricing scenarios.
04:36 Sam: Performance — can we run a microbenchmark? We want to know latency at 256 / 1024 token sequences and throughput with batching. Also important: cost per token estimates on your quantized models.
04:49 Marisol: We can provide a benchmark harness that measures p50/p95 token latency and throughput for your exact hardware. Two approaches: 1) remote perf tests against Redwood Dedicated variants to establish baseline, 2) onprem microbenchmarks using our harness that you run on the blades. For quantization we have 4‑bit and 8‑bit paths; results vary by model and sequence length.
05:12 Alex: Any off‑the‑shelf models you certify for the channel? Some customers want vetted open‑models out of box.
05:18 Diego: We maintain a model catalog with Redwood‑verified profiles — we'll share the compatibility matrix. Typical certified models for latency work are llama variants, phoenix‑lite, and a few tuned open decoders. For sensitive customers we recommend pinned model versions.
05:34 Sam: About network egress — some of our customers will insist on no egress to Redwood hosted control plane. Is Private truly air‑gapped?
05:42 Marisol: We have an on‑prem package that can run with a customer controlled control plane; in fully air‑gapped mode some features (like model catalog auto‑updates) are manual. We also support a hybrid mode where control plane is in your VPC. We'll document the differences.
05:58 Lina: For compliance we'll need: SOC2, ISO, encryption certs, and data residency info. Also will you allow us to do a security review and pen test?
06:06 Jamie: Yes — we'll hand over SOC2 reports under NDA and agree to a security review. Pen test coordination is possible — we'll need to schedule and set scope.
06:16 Priya: On integration level — what's required from the hardware vendor to become a validated partner? We assume a pre‑validation checklist.
06:23 Diego: Correct. The checklist includes: driver/kernel matrix, GPU topology diagram, expected OS image, network fabric details (RDMA/NIC versions), cooling/power constraints for high sustained throughput, and a short acceptance test (benchmarks pass thresholds).
06:38 Alex: Would you be open to embedding a small OEM tag or co‑brand for customers who buy hardware+software?
06:44 Jamie: Yes, co‑branding is common. We'll align on GTM and logos.
06:49 Priya: Any known incompatibilities with your runtime? We use a couple of custom NICs and a proprietary low‑latency driver in some SKUs.
06:57 Marisol: We may need to test those NICs — if they expose standard RDMA/NCCL stacks it's usually fine, but proprietary stacks sometimes require a shim. We'll add that to the checklist.
07:08 Sam: Ok. For the pilot — what would success criteria look like?
07:12 Jamie: Proposed pilot success metrics: p95 latency under X ms for 512 token sequences (we'll define X after the benchmark), throughput minimum of Y requests/sec under realistic batching, zero data egress outside customer network in Private mode, and automated provisioning with your orchestrator. Also a customer validation sign‑off.
07:33 Alex: That seems reasonable. We'd like a 6‑8 week pilot cadence.
07:36 Jamie: Great. For scheduling: Diego suggested a perf deep dive on Dec 20 where we share a test plan and you provide hardware access or we run remote tests.
07:45 Diego: I'll draft a test plan covering latency, KV cache behavior, multi‑node NCCL configs and quant path variations.
07:52 Priya: On commercial/partnering — we'll discuss preferred channel flow internally and come back with a recommendation (reseller vs managed onramp) by Dec 15.
07:59 Jamie: Perfect. A few practical asks now: Samir — can you drop the hardware spec and PCIe/NVLink topology in the shared folder? Also Lina, can you list initial compliance docs you'd like to see?
08:12 Sam: Yep I'll put specs in the shared drive (we'll send link).
08:16 Lina: I'll compile the compliance list and send to Jamie.
08:19 Jamie: Awesome. Any other blockers or questions?
08:23 Alex: One small thing: our customers sometimes ask for model fine‑tuning on their data — do you offer an integrated fine‑tune/run path or is that left to partners?
08:33 Diego: We have an integrations team and tooling for model fine‑tune, but for a channel we'd commonly recommend a partner‑managed fine tuning flow. We also support function calls/structured outputs for downstream tooling.
08:44 Priya: Sounds good.
08:47 Jamie: OK let's wrap up with next steps — I'll summarize: 1) Jamie to send partner playbook + pricing slides and SOC2 under NDA; 2) Marisol/Diego to produce technical test plan and perf harness; 3) Sam to share hardware specs; 4) Lina to share compliance list; 5) schedule Dec 20 tech deep dive. Anything to add?
09:10 Priya: No, that covers it. Thanks all.
09:14 Jamie: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by email with links and calendar invite for Dec 20.
09:18 Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: several proper nouns may be off (HeliosRotor occasionally mis‑transcribed as "Helio Rotor"), small audio drop at 00:45 produced a missed fragment, and some product names appeared as "Redwood Dedicate" in notes.

References mentioned: partner playbook (link to be shared), hardware spec sheet (shared drive), SOC2 (NDA).

Recap (in email style): Proposed 6‑8 week pilot; ship partner playbook + pricing; run hardware compatibility checklist; schedule technical deep dive 2028-12-20.
